title: The One Thing Standing In Your Way Of Having Your Dream Class ng-your-dream-class/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin argues that belief, not circumstance, is the single biggest obstacle to building the classroom a teacher wants, and offers a practical process for building that belief. He recommends creating and daily reviewing a vivid mental vision of one's ideal classroom, actively eliminating negative thoughts and excuses by replacing them with affirmations, deliberately seeking out positive-minded colleagues while avoiding the staff lounge's negativity, and consciously choosing to like and enjoy one's students regardless of difficulty. He closes by reframing the entire piece around purpose, arguing that teachers entered the profession to make a difference, not to complain, and that disciplined thinking is what turns that purpose into reality.
points: Belief that a dream class is achievable — not circumstance — is presented as the single largest obstacle for most teachers.
A daily visualization exercise, reviewing a vivid mental image of one's ideal classroom, is recommended as a concrete first step.
Negative thoughts and excuses should be actively replaced with affirmations like 'I can do this!' rather than indulged.
The staff lounge is described as a 'dangerous place' for negativity, and teachers are urged to seek out positive-minded colleagues instead.
Choosing to genuinely like one's students, even difficult ones, is framed as a deliberate decision that directly affects classroom management leverage.
quotes: The one thing standing in your way of creating the class you’ve always wanted is believing that you can.
You must first visualize your goal before in can become a reality. Keep a sharp image of your perfect class in your mind’s eye and review it daily—both before and after school.
Indulging in failures and disappointments and conjuring up justifications is as effortless as slipping into a warm bath.
The staff lounge is a dangerous place. The old adage that you should avoid it is spot on.
We didn’t get into teaching to snivel about students, complain with colleagues, or gin up excuses for ourselves. We got in it to make a difference.
